title: Blessings for Obedience, Curses for Rebellion
summary: Moses sets before Israel the covenant's sanctions. If the people obey, they will be blessed in city and field, in children, harvests, and herds, in victory and in standing among the nations. If they turn away, the same areas of life will be cursed, and the curses mount through disease, drought, defeat, and oppression to siege, famine so severe that parents eat their children, and scattering among the nations with no rest.
story: Chapter 28 is the climax of the covenant Moses has been laying out since chapter 5. The laws are finished (chapters 12-26), the ceremony at Ebal and Gerizim has been commanded (chapter 27), and now Moses spells out what is at stake. Only fourteen verses describe blessing; more than fifty describe curse. The imbalance is telling, because the rest of the Old Testament reads like a long commentary on this chapter. Israel's history in the books of Kings ends in the very siege, deportation, and scattering described here, first for the northern kingdom and then for Judah. The prophets quote and echo it constantly. Chapters 29 and 30 then look past the curse toward a promise of return and renewal.
historical:
Ancient treaties between a great king and his vassals commonly ended with lists of blessings for loyalty and curses for betrayal, called on by the gods who witnessed the treaty. Hittite treaties of the second millennium BC have this feature, and so do Assyrian loyalty oaths of the seventh century BC, especially the succession treaty of Esarhaddon from 672 BC, whose long list of curses includes some striking parallels to this chapter, among them the image of a sky like bronze and an earth like iron. Scholars who date Deuteronomy late often point to these parallels as evidence of its setting in Judah under Assyrian domination; those who date it early note that the treaty pattern is much older and widely shared.

The curses read, to many readers, like a description of what actually happened. The northern kingdom fell to Assyria in 722 BC and its people were deported. Jerusalem fell to Babylon in 587 or 586 BC after a long siege, and the book of Lamentations describes mothers eating their children in the famine (Lamentations 2:20; 4:10), as an earlier siege of Samaria had also produced (2 Kings 6:28-29). After Jerusalem's fall, a group of Judeans fled back to Egypt against Jeremiah's warning (Jeremiah 43). The first-century Jewish historian Josephus reports that after the Roman destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70, many captives were sent to labor in Egypt.
cultural:
The blessings and curses cover the whole of an Israelite's life: city and country (where people lived), the basket and kneading bowl (daily bread), children, herds, rain, and coming in and going out (every activity from morning to night). In a farming society without irrigation, rain in its season meant survival, and drought, locusts, blight, and mildew meant hunger. Being the head and not the tail, lending and not borrowing, meant national independence rather than subjection to foreign creditors.

The curses also reverse Israel's story. The diseases of Egypt return, the people who were as numerous as the stars become few, and the nation that came out of slavery is sent back to Egypt to be sold, with no one willing even to buy them. The foreign nation that swoops like an eagle, whose language Israel cannot understand, was a figure the prophets applied to Assyria and Babylon (Habakkuk 1:6-8 uses the eagle image for the Chaldeans, the Babylonians).
literary: The chapter is built in two unequal halves. Verses 1-14 give the blessings, framed by the condition if you faithfully obey. Verses 15-68 give the curses, framed by the matching condition if you do not obey. The blessings in verses 3-6 are mirrored almost word for word by the curses in verses 16-19, and the promise that enemies will flee in seven directions is reversed in verse 25. The curses then build in waves (verses 20-44, 45-57, and 58-68), each more severe than the last, moving from disease and drought to military defeat, from siege to cannibalism, and finally to exile and fear with no resting place. The final picture of a people saying in the morning, if only it were evening, and in the evening, if only it were morning, is one of the bleakest images in Scripture.

outline.t: Curses on daily life, health, and the land
Futile labor and an iron yoke
A nation from afar and the horrors of siege
Plagues, scattering, and a return to Egypt

doctrines.note: The covenant has real sanctions. Israel's life in the land depends on faithfulness to the LORD, and the chapter makes clear that the relationship cannot be treated lightly. Blessing and curse are the covenant's two possible futures.

God's judgment in this chapter is not arbitrary. It is the undoing of blessing, the reversal of the exodus, and the consequence of forsaking him. Verse 47 names the root: failing to serve the LORD with joy and gladness in abundance.

The LORD rules over rain, harvest, disease, and the movements of nations. He sends the blessing and he sends the enemy. History, in this chapter's view, is not a random sequence but the arena of God's covenant faithfulness.

words.note: Berakah, blessing. In the Old Testament blessing means the life-giving favor of God that shows itself in fruitfulness, security, and well-being. It goes back to God's first words to humanity in Genesis 1:28 and to his promise to Abraham in Genesis 12:2-3.

Qelalah, curse, the opposite of blessing. It means the withdrawal of God's favor and the experience of his judgment. The chapter lists curses in the same areas where blessings were promised, so that curse is blessing reversed.

Shama, to hear, here in the sense of obey. The chapter turns on whether Israel will listen to the voice of the LORD. In Hebrew thought, hearing and obeying are one act; to hear God truly is to do what he says, which is why the Shema (6:4) begins with this word.

Matsor, siege. The word appears in the refrain in the siege and distress that your enemy will inflict on you (verses 53, 55, and 57). Sieges were the most dreaded form of ancient warfare, starving a city into surrender, and they came to Samaria and Jerusalem exactly as the chapter warns.

christ: The New Testament reads the curse of the law in the light of the cross. Paul teaches that Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us, so that the blessing promised to Abraham might come to the nations (Galatians 3:13-14). Jesus himself, weeping over Jerusalem, foresaw a siege and destruction that echo the language of this chapter (Luke 19:41-44; 21:20-24), and that came in AD 70. The Beatitudes, which open the Sermon on the Mount with blessing after blessing (Matthew 5:3-12), can be read as a new covenant declaration in which blessing is given to the poor in spirit, the mourning, and the persecuted, not as a reward for success but as a gift of the kingdom. The connection is thematic: Jesus stands where Moses stood, before a people, setting out blessing, but he himself bears the curse.

hard.q: Does this chapter promise that faithful people will be healthy and wealthy, and that suffering is always a punishment?
hard.a:
The chapter promises national blessing and curse to Israel as a covenant people in the land. It is not a promise that every faithful individual will prosper or that every sufferer is being punished. The rest of the Old Testament makes that clear. Job is righteous and suffers terribly, and God rebukes the friends who insist his suffering must be punishment. Psalm 73 wrestles with the prosperity of the wicked, and Ecclesiastes observes that the righteous sometimes perish in their righteousness. Jesus rejects the assumption that a man was born blind because of sin (John 9:1-3).

Christians have read the chapter in several ways. Some stress that its blessings and curses belonged to Israel's national covenant under the law, fulfilled in Israel's history and in Christ, who bore the curse. Others see continuing principles of God's moral government of nations. What the Bible as a whole will not support is the teaching, sometimes called the prosperity gospel, that faith guarantees material wealth and health. The New Testament promises its readers suffering in this life (John 16:33; Acts 14:22) and a blessing that is spiritual and eternal, anchored in Christ (Ephesians 1:3).

questions: Verse 47 says the curses come because Israel did not serve God with joy in its abundance. How does gratitude, or its absence, shape faithfulness in times of plenty?
The curses reverse the exodus and send Israel back toward Egypt. What does it look like when people drift back into the very bondage they were freed from?
How do you hold together this chapter's warnings with books like Job that show the righteous suffering? What do they teach you together?
